title: Funds warned over shift into 'riskier' assets
full_text:
Superannuation funds are piling into risky fixed-income assets such as high-yield bonds and private credit to cater to the needs of ageing members, but a big four banking chief says they may lack the skills to navigate a severe downturn.
The $4.5 trillion sector has been increasing its allocation to higher-yield fixed income, including private credit, after decades of shunning the asset class in favour of infrastructure and private equity.
But the heads of the nation's top super funds told Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at an annual roundtable hosted by The Australian Financial Review and Visy chairman Anthony Pratt that it was in their members' interests to lend money to risky companies.
Don Russell, chairman of the $410 billion AustralianSuper, said the fund had to build portfolios to deliver good returns but also a "measure of capital stability" and so was increasingly turning towards riskier corporate debt.
"The weight of money will be augmented by this need to reallocate the fund toward assets which have a measure of predictability," he said.
"We need to look at credit not just in terms of investment grade bonds, but credit in terms of leverage loans, high-yield [bonds] and private credit."
Russell said the fund had moved its private credit function out of private markets and into fixed income to build its overall capabilities.
Deanne Stewart, who heads the $230 billion Aware Super, said more members were worried about running out of money in their retirement, which was guiding more super funds to invest in corporate debt.
"If you look at the retirement portfolio, it's still a mirror of their accumulation portfolio," she said. "In time, that will change toward downside protection, much more income and credit."
Meanwhile, IFM Investors chairwoman Cath Bowtell said the $267 billion fund manager, which is owned by the largest superannuation funds, was experiencing "increased investor appetite for the riskier high yield" investments in energy and digital technology.
"Those strategies are increasingly being talked about, and that capability is one that investors are looking to us to have available to them," she said.
But Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller urged superannuation funds not to rush into corporate lending because this risked exposing their members to a sharp downturn.
"We have not had a good old-fashioned credit meltdown for a very long time," he said. "We're not match fit on what happens when you have serious levels of defaults."
Miller also said super funds, unlike banks, had limited experience in dealing with challenges associated with liquidity, in which assets had to be sold on short notice to meet obligations to members requiring access to their savings. "They're not equipped to deal with it in the same way the banks are, and that's the catch-up that needs to be worked on."
Private credit has been one of the fastest-growing asset classes in the past five years in Australia and internationally, as large and small investors seek income and capital stability, while more borrowers have been cut out of the highly regulated banking sector.
Its fast growth has led to fears about lax lending standards and resulted in increased regulatory scrutiny. The sector has also been in the headlines as retail investors have scrambled to withdraw their money from private credit funds.
Bowtell said the panic among retail investors was "a source of friction" that could damage appetite for private credit among institutions. "The public discourse around private credit and the role of retail investors, as opposed to institutional investors, creates some noise for chief investment officers and asset allocators in funds," she said.
